chunks: From him, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from ʿAlī al-ʿAmrakī ibn ʿAlī, from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said:
I asked him about a man who performed tawaf and then remembered that he was without wudu (ablution). He said: He breaks off his tawaf and does not count it.

Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said: These reports, even if they are unrestricted, or most of them indicate that he repeats the tawaf, we carry them upon the tawaf of obligation, because of what we have previously presented from the hadith of Muḥammad ibn Muslim, and because it differentiated the ruling of the two tawafs: the tawaf of obligation and the tawaf of supererogation. Ruling by what is detailed is more appropriate than ruling by what is general, and what follows further clarifies that.

key_terms.الْمُجْمَلِ: the general or less specific wording
key_terms.الْمُفَصَّلِ: the detailed, specifically explained report or ruling
key_terms.طَوَافِ النَّافِلَةِ: the supererogatory tawaf distinguished from obligatory tawaf
key_terms.طَوَافِ الْفَرِيضَةِ: the obligatory tawaf whose ruling is being specified here
key_terms.لَا يَعْتَدُّ بِهِ: it is not considered valid or counted
key_terms.وُضُوءٍ: ritual ablution required for purity before certain acts of worship

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if someone performs tawaf and then realizes he had no wudu (ablution)?
ai.summary: This hadith states that if a person performs tawaf and then remembers he was without wudu (ablution), that tawaf is not valid. Shaykh al-Ṭūsī then explains that such reports are understood to apply to obligatory tawaf, based on other narrations that distinguish between obligatory and supererogatory tawaf and on the principle of preferring the more detailed report over the general one.
